set.narration: Pip hops on. 16, 17, 18, 19, 20! He counted to 20.

was.narration: Pip hops to the end. 18, 19, 20! He counted to 20.

edits.reason: Card 5 ends at 15, so jumping to 18 told a child who only listens that counting skips 16 and 17.

set.narration: Five ducks stand in a line. The first duck is in place 1. What place is the last duck in? Type its place number.

was.narration: Five ducks stand in a line. The last duck is at what place? Type the number.

edits.reason: "What place" with a number answer could be heard as "how many ducks". Naming place 1 shows the answer is a place number.

set.narration: Lena wears player number 24 on her shirt. Does 24 tell how many, or is it a label?
set.why: A player number is a label for the player. It does not count anything.

was.narration: Lena wears player number 24 on her shirt. Does 24 tell how many, or is it a name?
was.why: A player number is like a name for the player. It does not count anything.

edits.reason: The story and tap-7 call this use a label. One word for one idea.

set.narration: One hand has 5 fingers. Mia counts the fingers on each hand by 5s. 5, 10, 15, 20. Each hand adds 5.

was.narration: One hand has 5 fingers. Mia counts hands by 5s. 5, 10, 15, 20. Each jump adds 5.

edits.reason: "Counts hands by 5s" names the wrong unit. Each hand adds 5 fingers.

set.narration: Compare the tens first. 34 has 3 tens. 28 has 2 tens. So 34 is greater than 28.

was.narration: Big numbers have more tens. 34 has 3 tens. 28 has 2 tens. So 34 is greater than 28.

edits.reason: "Big numbers have more tens" is a loose rule. Comparing tens first is the one the items use.

set.narration: Which list goes from greatest to least? Is it 9, 25, 40? Is it 40, 25, 9? Or is it 25, 40, 9?

was.narration: Which line is in order from greatest to least? Is it 9, 25, 40, or 40, 25, 9, or 25, 40, 9?

edits.reason: Three lists joined by commas ran together by ear. Each list now gets its own question.

set.narration: Sam has 23 stickers. Mia has 32 stickers. Which number is less, 23 or 32?

was.narration: Sam has 23 stickers. Mia has 32 stickers. Who has fewer? Is it 23 or 32?

edits.reason: "Who has fewer?" asks for a person, but the choices are numbers.

set.narration: A number plus 8 is the same as 8 + 11. What is the missing number?

was.narration: What number makes this true? Blank + 8 = 8 + 11.

edits.reason: The device read the word "Blank" aloud, which a 6-year-old hears as a word, not a missing number.

set.narration: Sam has 9 apples. Mia has 13. To find how many more Mia has, take 9 from 13. Mia has 4 more apples than Sam.

was.narration: Sam has 9 apples. Mia has 13. To find how many more, take 9 from 13. Mia has 4 more.

edits.reason: "Mia has 4 more" could be heard as Mia now holding 4 more apples.

set.narration: Mia picks 7 more apples. Now she has 20. She eats 8 of them. Take 8 from 20 to find how many are left.

was.narration: Now Mia has 20 apples. She eats 8 of them. Take 8 from 20 to find how many are left.

edits.reason: Mia went from 13 to 20 apples with no reason given.

set.narration: Tom has 9 grapes. He eats 4 of them. Which number sentence shows how many are left? Is it 9 + 4 = 13, or 9 - 4 = 5?

was.narration: Tom has 9 grapes. He eats 4 of them. How many are left? Is it 9 + 4 = 13, or 9 - 4 = 5?

edits.reason: The question asked for a number, but the choices are number sentences.

set.why: Each hop is 5. From 30, two hops make 40, and one more hop makes 45.

was.why: Hop 10 to get to 40. Then hop 5 more to 45.

edits.reason: "Hop 10" on a line with steps of 5 confused the hop count.

set.narration: What digit is in the tens place of 639?

was.narration: In the number 639, how many tens are there in the tens place?

edits.reason: "How many tens are there" could mean 63, the tens in all of 639.

set.why: Each row adds 7 more. Ten rows of 7 is 70, because 10 × 7 is 7 tens.

was.why: Each row adds 7 more. Ten rows of 7 is 70, because 10 times any number adds a zero.

edits.reason: "10 times any number adds a zero" breaks with decimals in later grades.
The narration says 4 × 5 while the screen showed 5 × 4.

set.narration: Mia fills 10 glasses. Each glass gets 1/2 cup of juice. How many cups of juice does she use?
set.why: Two glasses use 1 cup. 10 glasses make 5 pairs, so she uses 5 cups.

was.narration: Mia fills 9 glasses. Each glass gets 1/2 cup of juice. How many cups of juice does she use? Type it as a decimal.
was.why: Two glasses use 1 cup. So 8 glasses use 4 cups. One more half cup makes 4.5.

edits.reason: The answer 4.5 needed decimals, which Ontario teaches in Grade 4. Groups of one half stay, with a whole-number total.

set.narration: The frog starts at 0. It makes 6 hops of 1/2. Drag the frog to where it lands.
set.why: Two hops of 1/2 make 1. Six hops make 3 groups of 1, so the frog lands on 3.

was.narration: The frog starts at 0. It makes 7 hops of 1/2. Drag the frog to where it lands.
was.why: Two hops of 1/2 make 1. Six hops make 3. One more half lands on 3.5.

edits.reason: Landing on 3.5 needed decimals, which Ontario teaches in Grade 4.

set.narration: The frog starts at 4. It hops back 1/2 each time. It makes 4 hops back. Drag the frog to where it lands.
set.why: Two hops of 1/2 make 1. Four hops back make 2, so the frog lands on 2.

was.narration: The frog starts at 4. It hops back 1/2 each time. It makes 5 hops back. Drag the frog to where it lands.
was.why: Five hops of 1/2 is 2 and a half. Going back from 4 lands on 1.5.

edits.reason: Landing on 1.5 needed decimals, which Ontario teaches in Grade 4.

set.narration: Here is the rule. Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number, and you get an equivalent fraction. Divide both by a number that goes into each evenly, and you get one too.

was.narration: Here is the rule. Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number, and you get an equivalent fraction. Divide both by the same number, and you get one too.

edits.reason: "Divide both by the same number" left out that it must divide both evenly.

set.narration: Move the frog to 7/4 on the number line.

was.narration: Move the frog to 7/4 on the number line. That is the same as 1 3/4.

edits.reason: The second sentence gave the answer away as 1 3/4.

set.narration: The line runs from 0 to 0.5 in steps of 5 hundredths. Move the frog to 0.35.

was.narration: The line runs from 0 to 0.5 in steps of one hundredth times five. Move the frog to 0.35.

edits.reason: "Steps of one hundredth times five" was hard to follow by ear.

set.narration: Four friends share this pizza. It has 4 equal slices. One slice is shaded. What part of the pizza does each friend get? Is it 1/4, 1/2, or 3/4?

was.narration: Four friends share this whole pizza equally. It is cut into 4 equal slices. What part of the pizza does each friend get? Is it 1/4, 1/2, or 3/4?

edits.reason: All 4 slices were shaded while the question asked for one friend's part.

set.narration: Zed ate the shaded halves of toast. How many halves did Zed eat? Is it 10, 6, or 5?

was.narration: Zed ate 5 halves of toast. Here is the toast. How many halves did Zed eat? Is it 10, 6, or 5?

edits.reason: The narration said "5 halves", so the child didn't need to count the picture.

set.narration: Frog hops one half at a time. It makes 8 hops from 0. Move the frog to where it lands.
set.why: Two hops of one half make 1. Eight hops make 4 groups of 2 hops, so the frog lands on 4.

was.narration: Frog hops one half at a time. It makes 7 hops from 0. Move the frog to where it lands.
was.why: Two hops of one half make 1. Six hops reach 3. One more half hop lands on 3 and a half.

edits.reason: Landing on 3.5 needed decimals, which Grade 2 doesn't use.

set.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. 5 sixths of it are still there. Ben eats 2 sixths. How much is left now? Is it 3/6, 7/6, 3/12, or 2/6?

was.narration: A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. 5 sixths of the pizza are left, and Ben eats 2 sixths. How much is left? Is it 3/6, 7/6, 3/12, or 2/6?

edits.reason: "Left" came twice in one question and was hard to follow by ear.

set.narration: A pizza has 4 equal slices. 2 slices are shaded. Which is the same amount as the 2 shaded slices? Is it one half, one fourth, or one whole?

was.narration: A pizza has 4 equal slices. 2 slices are shaded. Which is the same amount? Is it one half, one fourth, or one whole?

edits.reason: "Which is the same amount?" didn't say the same as what.

set.narration: Which circle has 1/3 shaded? Is it 2 of 3 parts shaded, 1 of 3 parts shaded, or 1 of 2 parts shaded?

was.narration: Which circle has 1/3 shaded? Is it 1/3 of the circle, 2/3 of the circle, or 1/2 of the circle?

edits.reason: Each picture choice was read aloud as its fraction, so the child could match the words without reading the picture. Choices now say how many parts are shaded.

set.narration: Which rectangle shows 3/8? Is it 5 of 8 parts shaded, 3 of 5 parts shaded, or 3 of 8 parts shaded?

was.narration: Which rectangle shows 3/8? Is it 3/8 of the rectangle, 5/8 of the rectangle, or 3/5 of the rectangle?

edits.reason: Each picture choice was read aloud as its fraction, so the child could match the words without reading the picture. Choices now say how many parts are shaded.

set.narration: 3 granola bars are shared fairly among 4 friends. Which picture shows one friend's share? Is it 1 of 4 parts shaded, 2 of 3 parts shaded, 3 of 8 parts shaded, or 3 of 4 parts shaded?

was.narration: 3 granola bars are shared fairly among 4 friends. Each friend gets 3/4 of a bar. Which picture shows that? Is it 1/4 of the bar, 2/3 of the bar, 3/8 of the bar, or 3/4 of the bar?

edits.reason: Each picture choice was read aloud as its fraction, so the child could match the words without reading the picture. Choices now say how many parts are shaded.

set.narration: Which picture shows one third of a pizza? Is it 1 of 6 parts shaded, 1 of 3 parts shaded, or 1 of 2 parts shaded?
set.why: One third means 1 of 3 equal slices. The pizza cut into 3 slices with 1 shaded shows it.

was.narration: Which picture shows one third of a pizza? Is it 1/6 of the circle, 1/3 of the circle, or 1/2 of the circle?
was.why: One third means 1 of 3 equal slices. Only the middle kind of cut shows that.

edits.reason: Each picture choice was read aloud as its fraction, so the child could match the words without reading the picture. Choices now say how many parts are shaded.
